findings.title: One shared AddRef flag makes the cleanup release handles that were never AddRef'd.
findings.body:
`inheritedHandleRefsAdded` becomes true after the first successful `DangerousAddRef`, and the `finally` block then calls `DangerousRelease` on every entry in the list. Suppose a later entry is already disposed: its `DangerousAddRef` throws `ObjectDisposedException`, and the cleanup still releases that entry and every entry after it, none of which were AddRef'd. That drops a live handle's refcount to zero and closes the fd while its owner is still using it. A `null` entry throws `NullReferenceException` in the loop and again in `finally`. The Windows path skips null, invalid and closed handles, so the two platforms also behave differently.

Fix: snapshot the list once, keep a per-handle `bool[]` of successful AddRefs, release only those, and skip or reject null and invalid handles the same way Windows does.

findings.title: Cleanup can throw inside `finally` and leave `s_processStartLock` held forever.
Restricted starts that share a handle race on its inherit flag under the shared read lock.
findings.body: Restricted starts take only the read lock, so two of them can run at the same time. If both list the same `SafeHandle` (for example a shared pipe or log file), thread A can finish and call `CleanupHandles`, which clears `HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT`, while thread B is between its own `SetHandleInformation` and `CreateProcess`. B's `CreateProcess` then fails, because every handle in `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST` must be inheritable. Fix: refcount the per-handle inherit enablement, or serialize the steps that set and clear the flags.

findings.title: `EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT` is now set for every start, including `CreateProcessWithLogonW`.
findings.body:
`creationFlags` now always includes `EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT`, and `cb` is always `sizeof(STARTUPINFOEX)`, even when `InheritedHandles` is null. The same flags go to `CreateProcessWithLogonW` (the `UserName` path). That API documents `lpStartupInfo` as a plain `STARTUPINFO` and does not list `EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT` among its supported creation flags. Every start with `UserName` set may therefore fail with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`, which would be a regression for callers that never use the new property. Even if the call succeeds, the handle-list attribute is not honoured there, so the restriction is silently not applied. I could not confirm how seclogon reacts to this flag.

Fix: set the flag and the extended `cb` only when an attribute list is actually built and `CreateProcess` is the API being called. Reject or document `InheritedHandles` together with `UserName`.

findings.title: An empty inherit list sends a zero-sized `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST`, which Windows rejects.
findings.body:
`handleCount` can be 0 in two cases:
- `InheritedHandles = []` and no standard handles are given;
- all standard handles are invalid, for example `Console.OpenStandardInputHandle()` in a GUI or service process with no console, as in the new `CanRedirectToInheritedHandles(restrictHandles: true)` test.

`UpdateProcThreadAttribute` is then called with `cbSize == 0`. As far as I know, Windows rejects an empty handle list (`ERROR_BAD_LENGTH`/`ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`), so `Process.Start` throws `Win32Exception` exactly when the user asked to inherit nothing. Fix: when `handleCount == 0`, skip the attribute list and call `CreateProcess` with `bInheritHandles: false`.

held.title: The native handle buffer is sized from one `Count` read but filled by a separate, unchecked enumeration.
held.body: `handlesToInherit` is allocated from `inheritedHandles.Count` here. `PrepareHandleAllowList` then reads `Count` again for `handlesToRelease` and writes into the native buffer while it enumerates the list, with no bounds check. If the user-supplied `IList` changes between the two reads (another thread adds to it), or a custom `IList` yields more items than `Count` reports, `handlesToInherit[handleCount++]` writes past the `NativeMemory` allocation and corrupts the native heap. Fix: copy the list to an array once and use that snapshot for sizing, iteration and release, on both Windows and Unix.

held.title: `POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT` closes the child's fds 0–2 when no stdio fd is redirected.
held.body: With `POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT`, macOS closes every fd that no file action names. Standard fds are only named through `adddup2` when `stdinFd`/`stdoutFd`/`stderrFd != -1`. The loop below also explicitly skips fds 0–2 when calling `addinherit_np`. So when a stdio fd is passed as -1 (inherit the parent's), the child starts with that standard stream closed. The fork path does not do this, because it uses `close_range(3, ...)`. Fix: call `posix_spawn_file_actions_addinherit_np` for 0, 1 and 2 whenever the corresponding fd is -1. I could not see whether the managed caller ever passes -1 here.

held.title: `fdwalk()` runs in the child between `fork` and `exec`, where it is not async-signal-safe.
held.body: On illumos/Solaris, `fdwalk` lists `/proc/self/fd` through `opendir`/`readdir`, which allocate memory. In a multithreaded parent, the child created by `fork`/`vfork` may only call async-signal-safe functions. If another thread held the malloc lock at fork time, the child deadlocks before `exec`, and `Process.Start` hangs waiting on the exec pipe. Fix: use an async-signal-safe approach, such as looping `fcntl` up to the `RLIMIT_NOFILE` value captured before the fork, or `closefrom`-style syscalls.
